doc.title: Chuck Mancuso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Buffalo, New York, October 10, 2013

title: Race counts in Mancuso's chart of stars and Crouch's claim
summary: Rowe asks about the racial makeup of his mainstream and underground star lists and Crouch's view that whites took the music.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Because I had to remind myself, this is the son. Because he’s sitting there with a tenor sax. Well we’re about to run out of tape here. But I wanted to — one more chart you have, Mainstream Stars from 1900 to 1950 and Underground Stars.

Yeah you did. Under Mainstream Stars we have, I counted this, there was like 15 white people and almost all male. And under Underground Stars there were 12 black people and 5 white people. Does that say something?
I don’t know. I don’t know what I was thinking. What were they, Ruby Braff?
Well these were no, big names. The big names. People who we’d recognize. And I wasn’t going to draw any conclusions from it. But it just seemed like if a fellow like Stanley
Crouch said that the white musicians had absconded with most of our musical styles, is he correct in that, in your estimation?

Oh I don’t know. There’s a sensitivity on his part. I mean he’s always been contentious about some of the whites. And you know, a lot of the people that owned the record companies were white. And I think they felt more comfortable dealing with them, some of them might have been prejudiced, I mean I don’t think that Norman Granz was, and I don’t know about Gibson, with Concord, his tend to be white, with Betty Carter and a couple of the others. But that was a while ago when I did that, so I don’t —
Well you didn’t say that so I don’t want to put that spin —
It wasn’t done consciously. I don’t know why I chose who I chose. I can’t even remember what I did back then.
